title: THE SERPENT IN EDEN BECAME THE DRAGON IN REVELATION—BUT THE ENEMY NEVER SAW THE CROSS COMING
paragraphs: THE SERPENT IN EDEN BECAME THE DRAGON IN REVELATION—BUT THE ENEMY NEVER SAW THE CROSS COMING

He entered the Bible whispering beneath a tree. He leaves it defeated before the throne of God. And between those two moments lies the greatest rescue story ever told—a story that reveals why Satan changes his tactics, why humanity keeps falling for his lies, and why Jesus Christ is the only One who can break the curse.
There is something terrifying about the way evil first enters the biblical story.
No thunder.
No army marching across the horizon.
No monstrous creature breathing fire.
Just a serpent.
A question.
And a woman standing in a garden where nothing had ever died.
“Did God really say…?”
That was all it took to begin the conversation that would change human history.
Now travel to the final book of the Bible.
The garden is gone. The innocence is shattered. Kingdoms have risen and fallen. Blood has stained the earth. Generations have lived beneath the shadow of sin and death.
And suddenly, the serpent is no longer presented merely as a cunning creature in a garden.
He is described as a great red dragon.
Seven heads. Ten horns. A tail sweeping stars from heaven. A furious enemy making war against those who belong to God.
Why does Satan appear as a serpent in Genesis but as a dragon in Revelation?
Did he grow stronger?
Did his nature change?
Was the serpent only the beginning of something far more horrifying?
Or is Scripture showing us something deeper about deception, rebellion, spiritual warfare, and the victory of Jesus Christ?
Because the answer is not merely about Satan.
It is about the lie that entered your life quietly.
The temptation you thought you could control.
The shame you have carried for years.
The sin that started as a whisper and eventually felt like a monster you could no longer defeat.
And above all, it is about the Savior who walked into the battlefield, took the curse upon Himself, and accomplished what no human being could ever accomplish.
But to understand the dragon, we must return to the serpent.
And to understand the serpent, we must first remember what humanity lost.
Genesis opens with a world that God repeatedly declares good.
There was no graveyard in Eden.
No hospital waiting room.
No marriage collapsing under betrayal.
No mother burying her child.
No person staring into a mirror wondering whether they were beyond forgiveness.
Human beings were created in God's image, blessed with dignity, responsibility, relationship, and the privilege of living under their Creator's goodness.
Then Genesis 3 introduces a disturbing presence.
The Hebrew text begins:
וְהַנָּחָשׁ הָיָה עָרוּם
Veha-nachash hayah arum.
“Now the serpent was more crafty…”
The Hebrew word נָחָשׁ (nachash) means “serpent” or “snake.”

The word עָרוּם (arum) describes someone or something crafty, shrewd, or cunning. Depending on context, related language can describe prudence or deceptive cleverness. Here, the serpent's behavior reveals its sinister purpose.
And there is a remarkable literary detail.
In Genesis 2:25, Adam and Eve are described as naked and unashamed. The Hebrew word for naked, arummim, sounds strikingly similar to the word arum, crafty, in Genesis 3:1.
The innocent humans are naked.
The serpent is crafty.
The text places vulnerability beside cunning.
And the enemy approaches not by announcing war, but by questioning the Word of God.
“Did God actually say…?” (Genesis 3:1, ESV)
Notice what the serpent does not say.
He does not begin by declaring, “I am here to destroy you.”
He does not reveal the devastating consequences of disobedience.
He does not explain the pain, alienation, and death that will follow.
He begins by making God's command seem questionable.
Then restrictive.
Then unreasonable.
Then untrustworthy.
And suddenly, the forbidden fruit looks less like rebellion and more like freedom.
That is how deception works.
It rarely introduces itself as destruction.
It arrives disguised as an opportunity.
A private conversation that feels harmless.
A compromise nobody will notice.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from God, but you keep telling yourself you can handle it.
A secret habit that promises relief while quietly tightening its grip.
A little resentment you keep feeding because forgiveness feels unfair.
A desire to control your own life because surrender to God feels frightening.
And the serpent's ancient question begins echoing inside a modern heart.
Did God really say?
Did God really say you must forgive?
Did God really say you must flee sexual immorality?
Did God really say you cannot serve both God and money?
Did God really say you must deny yourself and follow Christ?
Did God really say obedience matters when nobody is watching?
The scenery changes.
The temptation changes.
But the attack on God's truth remains painfully familiar.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part of Eden is that the serpent did not need to create a new world.
He only needed to convince humanity to distrust the God who had already given them everything they needed.
That is the scandal of Genesis 3.
Humanity was surrounded by divine generosity, yet reached for what God had forbidden.
Adam and Eve were responsible for their disobedience. The serpent deceived, but temptation did not erase human accountability.
And when their eyes were opened, the promised freedom did not arrive.
Shame arrived.
Fear arrived.
Hiding arrived.
Blame arrived.
The first human response to sin was not a celebration of independence.
It was an attempt to cover nakedness and escape the presence of God.
How many of us are still living that same story?
We sin.
We hide.
We make excuses.
We promise to change.
We fail again.
Then we convince ourselves that if God saw everything we have done, He would want nothing to do with us.
But Scripture tells us something astonishing.
After Adam and Eve sinned, God came looking for them.
“Where are you?” (Genesis 3:9)
The all-knowing God was not asking because He had lost their location.
The question confronted them with the reality of their hiding.
And that same question reaches into the places we would rather keep locked.
Where are you?
Not the version of yourself you post online.
Not the person everyone at church assumes you are.
Not the smiling face covering an exhausted spirit.
Where are you when the lights go out and the truth becomes impossible to avoid?
And here is where the story begins to turn.
Because in the very chapter where sin enters human history, God announces a conflict that will end in the serpent's defeat.
Genesis 3:15 contains one of Scripture's most important promises.
God declares that there will be enmity between the serpent and the woman, between their offspring, and that the woman's offspring will strike the serpent's head while the serpent strikes his heel.
The Hebrew includes these words:
הוּא יְשׁוּפְךָ רֹאשׁ וְאַתָּה תְּשׁוּפֶנּוּ עָקֵב
Hu yeshufkha rosh, ve'attah teshufennu aqev.
A close rendering is:
“He shall strike your head, and you shall strike his heel.”
The Hebrew verb shuf is commonly rendered “strike” or “bruise,” and its precise nuance is debated. The image nevertheless presents a conflict involving wounds to the head and heel.
Christians have long understood this verse as the protoevangelium, meaning the first announcement or foreshadowing of the Gospel.
That does not mean Genesis 3:15 explicitly names Jesus or explains the crucifixion in advance.
It means that, read within the full unfolding story of Scripture, this promise points toward the ultimate victory accomplished through Christ.
The serpent would not have the final word.
Sin would not have the final word.
Death would not have the final word.
And the God whom humanity had disobeyed was already revealing that evil would not reign forever.
Think about that.
Before humanity had learned how to build an altar, God had spoken of the serpent's defeat.
Before Israel became a nation, the promise was there.
Before Bethlehem, before Golgotha, before the empty tomb, Scripture had begun telling the story of a coming victory.
And that brings us to a detail many readers overlook.
Genesis 3 never explicitly calls the serpent “Satan.”
The Hebrew narrative calls him the serpent.
It describes his craftiness and his temptation, but does not directly identify him by the name Satan in that chapter.
That identification becomes explicit in the New Testament.
Revelation 12:9 declares:
“And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world…” (ESV)
Read that again.
The great dragon.
The ancient serpent.
The devil.
Satan.
Four descriptions brought together in one verse.
The Greek text says:
ὁ δράκων ὁ μέγας, ὁ ὄφις ὁ ἀρχαῖος
Ho drakōn ho megas, ho ophis ho archaios.
“The great dragon, the ancient serpent.”
The word ὄφις (ophis) means serpent or snake.
The word δράκων (drakōn) means dragon, a term used in ancient Greek for a great serpent or fearsome serpent-like creature.
These words are related in imagery, but Revelation is doing more than describing an animal.
It is unveiling the identity and character of the enemy through apocalyptic symbolism.
The serpent associated with the beginning of humanity's fall is identified with the dragon portrayed as the enemy of God's people.
The same adversary.
The same opposition to God.
The same deceiving purpose.
But a dramatically different literary setting.
And this is where biblical accuracy matters.
The Bible does not teach that Satan physically evolved from a small snake into a giant dragon.
Genesis is presenting the temptation in Eden.
Revelation is using prophetic, apocalyptic imagery to unveil the cosmic dimensions of evil and its opposition to God's kingdom.
The dragon is not evidence that Satan underwent a biological transformation or grew seven literal heads.
The heads, horns, and other features belong to Revelation's symbolic world, which draws heavily from the Old Testament's imagery of terrifying beasts and hostile empires.
The difference between serpent and dragon is therefore not a biblical account of Satan changing species.
It is a difference in how Scripture portrays his work.
In Eden, the focus is intimate deception.
In Revelation, the vision exposes the terrifying scope of his rebellion, accusation, persecution, and defeat.
And the imagery is not random.
Long before John received the visions recorded in Revelation, the Old Testament had used monstrous serpent and dragon-like imagery to portray threatening powers.
Isaiah 27:1 speaks of Leviathan, the fleeing and twisting serpent, and of the dragon in the sea.
Psalm 74:13–14 recalls God's victory over the sea monsters and Leviathan.
In Ezekiel 29:3, Pharaoh is portrayed as a great monster lying in the midst of his rivers.
These passages arise in different historical and literary contexts, and they should not all be treated as literal descriptions of Satan.
Yet together they show how Scripture uses monstrous creatures to communicate the arrogance, danger, and apparent strength of forces opposing God's rule.
Revelation draws upon this biblical world of imagery.
The dragon represents more than an unsettling creature.
He is the adversary who opposes the Messiah, deceives the nations, accuses God's people, and wages war against those who belong to Christ.
But here is the detail that changes everything.
The dragon in Revelation is terrifying, but he is never presented as equal to God.
Satan is not God's opposite in power.
He is not an eternal rival who possesses the same authority as the Creator.
Christian Scripture presents God alone as the sovereign Creator.
Satan is a rebellious creature whose activity remains subject to divine judgment and whose defeat is certain within the vision of Revelation.
And that matters because some Christians have developed a picture of spiritual warfare that gives the devil far more attention than Scripture gives him.
They live as though Jesus and Satan are locked in a contest whose outcome remains uncertain.
As though heaven is anxiously waiting to discover who will win.
As though one more demonic attack could somehow overthrow the finished work of Christ.
But Revelation does not end with the dragon sitting on a throne.
It ends with God and the Lamb reigning.
The enemy may rage.
He may deceive.
He may accuse.
He may persecute.
But he cannot overthrow the sovereign purpose of God.
And when Revelation 12 opens its heavenly vision, something extraordinary appears.
A woman.
A male child.
A dragon waiting to devour the child.
The woman and child are presented through imagery rich with connections to Israel, the Messiah, and the people of God.
The child is described as the One destined to rule the nations with a rod of iron, language echoing Psalm 2 and pointing to Jesus Christ.
The dragon stands ready to destroy.
Yet the child is caught up to God and to His throne.
The vision compresses the Messiah's victory and exaltation into powerful symbolic scenes.
It does not give us a detailed chronological account of every event in Jesus' earthly life.
Then war breaks out in heaven.
Michael and his angels fight against the dragon.
The dragon and his angels fight back.
But they do not prevail.
The dragon is thrown down.
And heaven announces the arrival of salvation, power, the kingdom of God, and the authority of His Christ.
Then comes one of the most extraordinary statements in the entire book.
Revelation 12:11 says:
“And they have conquered him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony…” (ESV)
Not by their personal perfection.
Not by their social influence.
Not by the number of people who admired them.
Not by pretending they had never struggled.
By the blood of the Lamb.
The Greek expression is:
διὰ τὸ αἷμα τοῦ ἀρνίου
Dia to haima tou arniou.
“Because of” or “through the blood of the Lamb.”

The Greek preposition dia with the accusative can express the grounds or reason for something. In this verse, the blood of the Lamb is central to the believers' victory, alongside their testimony and their willingness to remain faithful even in the face of death.
Do not miss the significance.
The dragon is not ultimately overcome because Christians become impressive enough to frighten him.
He is overcome through the saving victory of Jesus Christ, the Lamb who was slain.
The title “Lamb” is especially powerful.
Because what kind of Savior defeats a dragon by becoming a sacrificial Lamb?
What kind of King conquers through a cross?
What kind of Lord wins by laying down His life?
The answer is the Jesus revealed in the Gospel.
The world celebrates strength that crushes enemies.
Jesus reveals divine victory through obedient, self-giving love.
The world admires kings who preserve their lives at any cost.
Jesus willingly gave His life to save sinners.
The world assumes that humiliation means defeat.
But the cross, which looked like the greatest humiliation imaginable, became the place where Christ triumphed over the powers of evil.
Colossians 2:14–15 connects Christ's cross with the cancellation of the record of debt against us and His triumph over the rulers and authorities.
Hebrews 2:14–15 explains that through death Jesus acted to destroy the one who has the power of death, identified there as the devil, and to deliver those enslaved by the fear of death.
The victory of Christ is not a motivational metaphor.
It is the center of Christian redemption.
And here is the part that may hurt before it heals.
Satan's greatest weapon against many believers is not always the temptation that comes before sin.
Sometimes it is the accusation that comes afterward.
Before the sin, the whisper says:
It is not that serious.
After the sin, the accusation says:
You are beyond forgiveness.
Before the compromise:
Nobody will know.
After the compromise:
If they knew, they would never love you.
Before the fall:
You can always repent later.
After the fall:
Your repentance could never be sincere.
The same enemy who tempts is identified in Revelation 12:10 as the accuser of God's people.
And perhaps you know what it feels like to live under accusation.
You remember what you did.
The person you betrayed.
The marriage you damaged.
The years you wasted.
The addiction you concealed.
The words you wish you could take back.
The prayer you stopped praying because you felt too ashamed to approach God.
You have heard sermons about forgiveness.
You know the verses.
You can explain grace to somebody else.
But when it comes to your own story, you wonder whether the blood of Jesus is truly enough.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was harmless.
It says your sin was so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
But it also says His sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who comes to Him in genuine faith.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” (ESV)
No condemnation.
Not because your past has been imaginary.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because holiness no longer matters.
But because Jesus Christ bore the judgment sin deserved and rose victorious from the grave.
Grace does not make sin beautiful.
Grace makes redemption possible.
And genuine grace does not leave us comfortably enslaved to the things Christ died to free us from.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is the fitting response of a heart being turned back toward God.
And this is where the ancient serpent's story becomes intensely personal.
The enemy wants you to believe that because you fell, you belong to him.
But the Gospel announces that those who belong to Christ have been redeemed at a price.
Your failure is real.
Your accountability is real.
The consequences of some choices may remain painfully real.
But for those who repent and trust in Jesus, sin does not possess the final authority to define their identity before God.
Jesus does.
Perhaps you are reading this while fighting a battle nobody else knows about.
You still attend church, but your private life has become a place of compromise.
You still post Bible verses, but you have not opened your Bible in weeks.
You still tell everyone you are fine, but you feel spiritually numb.
You still believe in Jesus, yet some part of you is afraid that you have wandered too far.
You keep remembering the person you used to be.
The promises you made.
The prayers you prayed.
The day you said you would never go back.
And yet somehow, you went back.
Maybe more than once.
Maybe so many times that the thought of beginning again feels exhausting.
If that is you, do not confuse the voice of accusation with the voice of the Shepherd.
Conviction calls you to turn from sin and return to God.
Accusation seeks to bury you beneath hopelessness.
The Holy Spirit's work is never to make rebellion feel safe. But neither does Scripture teach that a repentant sinner must remain trapped in despair.
First John 1:9 assures believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
And Jesus Himself says in John 6:37:
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” (ESV)
Whoever.
Not merely the person with a respectable testimony.
Not merely the Christian who has never fallen publicly.
Not merely the believer whose family looks perfect.
Whoever comes to Him.
That invitation is not permission to cherish sin.
It is an invitation to abandon our hiding and come to the only Savior who can forgive and transform us.
And now we must return to Revelation, because the dragon's story contains another uncomfortable truth.
A defeated enemy can still be dangerous.
Revelation 12:12 portrays the devil as furious because he knows his time is short.
First Peter 5:8 warns believers to remain sober-minded and watchful because the devil prowls like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
James 4:7 instructs Christians to submit themselves to God, resist the devil, and trust that he will flee.
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
The Christian life is not a call to become obsessed with demons.
It is a call to remain faithful to Christ.
We resist deception by holding fast to truth.
We resist temptation by walking in obedience and relying on God's grace.
We resist accusation by remembering the Gospel.
We resist spiritual compromise through repentance, prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and the strengthening work of the Holy Spirit.
And we must be careful not to blame every human struggle on Satan.
Scripture also speaks of the world, the flesh, our own desires, and the responsibility we bear for our choices.
Not every hardship is a direct demonic attack.
Not every illness is caused by an evil spirit.
Not every anxious thought is evidence that the devil is speaking.
Biblical spiritual warfare requires discernment, not sensationalism.
But there is a real enemy.
And he is not interested in helping you become more like Jesus.
He would rather have you doubt God's goodness, normalize your compromise, despise your neighbor, and abandon the hope of the Gospel.
Yet even the dragon's fury cannot cancel the victory of the Lamb.
And Revelation does not leave the enemy's future uncertain.
In Revelation 20:10, the devil is thrown into the lake of fire.
This scene belongs to Revelation's final judgment vision, and Christians differ over the precise chronology of the events surrounding Revelation 20.
But the central truth is unmistakable.
Satan's opposition to God does not continue forever.
Evil will be judged.
The devil will not reign eternally over God's creation.
The dragon does not get the final chapter.
Then Revelation 21 announces something almost too beautiful to comprehend.
A new heaven.
A new earth.
God dwelling with His people.
Tears wiped away.
Death no more.
Mourning no more.
Crying no more.
Pain no more.
The former things passed away.
Do you see the breathtaking movement of Scripture?
In Genesis, humanity loses access to the tree of life.
In Revelation, the tree of life appears again, bearing fruit and associated with the healing of the nations.
In Genesis, sin brings alienation, shame, and death.
In Revelation, God dwells with His redeemed people, and death is abolished.
In Genesis, the serpent deceives humanity.
In Revelation, the ancient serpent faces final judgment.
In Genesis, humanity hides from God.
In Revelation, God's servants see His face.
And at the center of that entire story stands Jesus Christ.
The promised offspring.
The obedient Son.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The reigning Lamb.
The coming King.
The One who does not merely repair a damaged life but brings His people into the hope of new creation.
This is why the Bible's movement from serpent to dragon is so profound.
The imagery expands from a garden encounter to a cosmic conflict.
But the greater revelation is not how frightening the enemy appears.
It is how completely God accomplishes redemption through His Son.
The serpent whispered that disobedience would bring freedom.
Jesus declared that the truth would set people free.
The serpent invited humanity to distrust the Father's word.
Jesus trusted and obeyed the Father, even unto death.
The serpent's deception led humanity into shame.
Jesus endured the shame of the cross to bring sinners into reconciliation with God.
The dragon makes war against God's people.
The Lamb secures their ultimate victory.
And the cross stands as the dividing line between the enemy's accusations and the believer's hope.
Maybe you began reading this because you were curious about a biblical mystery.
Why a serpent?
Why a dragon?
Why two images for the same adversary?
But perhaps the deeper question is not what Satan looks like in biblical symbolism.
Perhaps it is this:
Whose voice have you been listening to?
The voice that tells you God's commands are cruel?
The voice that tells you your secret sin is harmless?
The voice that tells you your shame is permanent?
The voice that tells you there is no point in trying to follow Jesus anymore?
Or the voice of the Savior who calls sinners to repentance and offers forgiveness through His finished work?
Because you can know the Greek word for dragon and still be deceived.
You can explain Hebrew grammar and still refuse to surrender your heart.
You can win arguments about Revelation while losing your appetite for prayer, holiness, and love.
Biblical knowledge is precious.
But knowledge that never leads us toward faith, worship, obedience, and love has missed its deepest purpose.
Jesus did not give His life merely so that we could become experts in the symbolism of the enemy.
He gave His life to save sinners and reconcile them to God.
And if the Holy Spirit is exposing something in your heart right now, do not run from that conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Seek forgiveness where you have caused harm.
Ask for help from mature believers when the battle has become too heavy to carry alone.
Return to the Scriptures.
Return to prayer.
Return to fellowship.
Above all, come to Jesus Christ.
Not because you have finally become worthy of His mercy.
But because He is the only Savior who can give it.
And if you have never trusted in Him, do not mistake religious familiarity for saving faith.
The invitation of the Gospel is to repent and believe in Jesus Christ, who died for sins and rose again.
The answer to the serpent is not human pride.
The answer to the dragon is not human strength.
The answer is the Lamb.
And there is something beautiful about what happens when a redeemed person begins to tell the truth about what Jesus has done.
The shame that once demanded silence becomes a testimony of grace.
The person who once hid in darkness begins to walk in the light.
The believer who once thought the battle was hopeless begins encouraging others to endure.
Not because every struggle disappears overnight.
Not because every wound heals on our preferred schedule.
But because the risen Christ is faithful, and His people are not left without hope.
That is why I want to ask you something personal.
You do not need to share private details or confess publicly what should be handled in a safe, appropriate setting.
Or simply write:
Not as a performance for other people.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But as a small, honest reminder that you are not the only person who needs the mercy and strength of Jesus.
And if you have experienced God's forgiveness after a season of rebellion, perhaps your testimony can encourage somebody who believes restoration is impossible.
There may be someone reading the comments tonight who is desperately searching for a reason not to give up.
Your words could point them back to Christ.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Think of that friend who once loved the Lord but has slowly drifted away.
That family member who believes their past is too ugly for God to forgive.
That young believer who has been frightened by sensational teachings about Satan but has never truly understood the victory of Jesus.
That person who does not yet believe, but has been quietly wondering whether God could ever receive someone like them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to expose their struggles.
But to invite them to see the hope found in Jesus Christ.
Our desire is to keep bringing Scripture-centered teaching, Gospel encouragement, biblical understanding, and practical discipleship to people who need more than another passing inspirational quote.
We want to help people know Jesus, understand His Word, repent where repentance is needed, grow in grace, and remain faithful through life's battles.
Those free resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and discipleship accessible to as many people as possible.
And for those who believe in this mission and want to help it continue, I want to extend a sincere invitation.

If you regard supporting Gospel-centered ministry as part of your Christian giving, you may prayerfully include it in your regular giving. Some believers may choose to treat such support as an offering or as part of their personal tithing practice, according to their convictions and church commitments.
But let us be clear about something important.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ, not something purchased by a monthly payment.
And supporting an online ministry should never become an excuse to neglect the responsibilities you have toward your local church, your family, or those in genuine need.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be decided in the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
These items are simply an additional expression of appreciation. The heart of the mission remains the Gospel, not merchandise.
And if you cannot contribute financially, you are still welcome here.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep growing.
Keep pointing people to Jesus.
And that brings us back to the question that started everything.
Why does Satan appear as a serpent in Genesis but a dragon in Revelation?
Because Scripture first shows us the enemy's deception in a garden, then unveils the wider conflict of his opposition to God and His people.
The imagery changes.
The biblical perspective widens.
The full horror of evil becomes visible.
But the final revelation is not that Satan is more powerful than we imagined.
It is that Jesus Christ is victorious over an enemy no human being could defeat alone.
The serpent's lie did not overturn God's promise.
The dragon's rage cannot overthrow God's throne.
The cross was not the end of Jesus.
The tomb could not hold Him.
And the future does not belong to the accuser.
It belongs to the King of kings and Lord of lords.
So tonight, if you are tired of hiding, come to Christ.
If you have fallen, repent and return.
If you are weary, bring your burdens to Him.
If you are afraid, remember whose hands hold your future.
If you are standing, remain humble and watchful.
If you have been forgiven, extend mercy to others.
And if you are wondering whether the story of your life can still be redeemed, look not to the size of your failure but to the sufficiency of the Savior.
The first pages of Scripture show humanity hiding among the trees.
The Gospel shows Jesus bearing our sins upon a tree.
And the final pages of Scripture show God's redeemed people welcomed into a creation where the curse will be no more.
What began with scandal in a garden is answered by grace through a cross and fulfilled in the victory of the risen King.
The serpent may have taught humanity how to hide in shame, but the Lamb has opened the way for sinners to come home.
